title: The nine goals and the thirteen weeks
bridge: The quarter plan is like a release plan with nine epics, each a list of tickets with owners and days. Except: the goals depend on each other in a fixed order, walls first. A late ticket in G0 or G3 moves every goal that runs agents.
intro: The platform is built in thirteen weeks by nine goals, G0 to G8. This lesson names each goal, what it delivers and when. It also explains why the order is walls first, runtime second, agents third.

picture.caption: Every goal feeds the Nova pilot; G0 and G3 must come first.

steps.text: the GitHub App, the gateway and the approval check exist before any agent runs
the runtime is proven by drills in W9; the fcp pilot starts in W9 to W10
routines run on the same harness, VMs and walls as Nova
cost, speed and quality are measured from the first run
Byte reviews Nova's draft PRs from W8
fast, honest checks are how Nova proves its work
skills and brain pages teach agents and people the same facts

p: The quarter starts on 1 October 2026. Week 1 (W1) is 1 to 7 October, W2 is 8 to 14 October, and W13 ends on 30 December. Every ticket names its weeks.
There are 242 tickets with 287 days of work in total. A ticket is 0.5 to 3 days. Anything bigger was split into tickets that each deliver something usable.
sections.because: We read the planning fields first, because they say when the work happens, who does it, and what comes first.

notes.text: Goal code and a two-digit number, in the order the tickets can be built.
Who owns it: plat (Platform), devops, be, shai, guild (Guilds), sec (Security) or nave.
First and last week. [3, 3] means the work happens in W3, 15 to 21 October.
null for normal work. decide marks a meeting or a choice; stretch means only if time allows.
Tickets in the same goal that must land first.
Free text for what it needs from other goals. Here: the GitHub App from G0.

sections.h: G0 and G3: the front door and the house
p: G0, Guardrails and identity, runs W1 to W6: 19 tickets, 17 days. It writes down the review rules and turns on the fcp ruleset. It sets up the agents' Anthropic organization with one key per workload. It also creates the rhino-ai-agents GitHub App, the independent-approval check and the LLM gateway.
G0 also narrows the Vault role that CI uses. That must land before agents push branches, because fcp's backend CI runs on every push with CI's own credentials.

G3, Agent runtime, is the biggest goal: 42 tickets, 60 days, W2 to W9. It builds the repo, the AWS account, the network and the proxy. Then come Temporal, the broker, the image, the warm pools, the harness and the workflows.
G3 ends in W9 with failure drills. The last proof is one test ticket going from Slack to a draft PR, in a fresh VM with no key inside.

G4, Nova pilot, runs W6 to W12: 30 tickets, 32 days. It builds TICKET-BENCH, a fixed set of past fcp tickets to score Nova on. Then come the hand-off from Jira, the readiness check and the plan format. After them: checks first, the QA agent, the judges, Byte on drafts and the ready gate.
Nova first works on tickets of the ai-agents repo itself in W8 to W9. The fcp pilot starts in W9 to W10, with 5 to 10 small tickets chosen with the guilds.

G5, Routines, runs W3 to W12: 36 tickets, 32.5 days. A routine is Nova with a charter and a trigger: CI fixers, upgrade fixers, bug fixers, a dead-code remover. Each routine climbs a trust ladder: shadow first, then drafts to its owner, then normal.

sections.h: G1, G2 and G7: measure, review, test fast
p: G1, Telemetry and metrics, runs W2 to W12: 19 tickets, 17 days. It deploys a telemetry collector that drops content, a nightly metrics job, Grafana dashboards, and a developer survey in October and December.

G2, Review gate (Byte), runs W2 to W11: 17 tickets, 23.5 days. It builds BYTE-GOLD, a set of real past bugs to measure how good Byte's reviews are. Then it gates Byte's changes on that score and adds a review panel.
G7, Fast feedback, runs W3 to W12: 35 tickets, 51 days, mostly BE and DevOps. It gives fcp an API test layer with fakes, verify scripts, more linters, and FCP Lab smoke tests on every PR.

sections.h: G6 and G8: what agents and people know
p: G6, R&D brain, runs W1 to W11: 23 tickets, 30.5 days, mostly Shai. It writes 35 seed pages in the rnd-kb repo, each with an owner and a review date. It also builds a linter, a kb search tool, and a Slack bot that answers with citations.

G8, Skills and tools, runs W3 to W12: 21 tickets, 23.5 days. It creates the private plugin marketplace and the shared skills, such as plan-and-grill, verify and pr-story. It adds a plugin CI with an eval gate, and four trainings.
Walls come before agents. The GitHub App, the gateway, the approval check and the narrowed Vault role must exist before an agent pushes anything.
The runtime and the bench both come before the pilot. Then we can measure Nova before people depend on it. Routines come after Nova's harness, because they reuse it.
Some work starts early because it needs no agent: the ruleset, Renovate for dependencies, the brain's first pages, the API test layer. That keeps every team busy from W1.

callout.text: A goal that runs agents (G4, G5) can never start before the walls it relies on. If a G0 or G3 ticket slips, the pilot date moves; nobody turns a wall off to keep a date.

p: Platform owns most tickets, then DevOps, BE, Shai, the Guilds, Security and Nave. A ticket can list two teams when they work together, for example DevOps and Platform.
Three tickets are flagged decide: a choice with an owner, usually with no code. Nine are flagged stretch: we do them only if time allows. Everything else is planned work.

quiz.q: Why must G0's narrowing of the Vault CI role land before agents push branches?

options.text: Because fcp's backend CI runs on every push with CI's own credentials, so an agent's branch would run with them
options.why: cloud-ci, client-ci and sdk-ci run on push to any branch; the role must be narrow before agent branches exist.

options.text: Because the Vault role is where the agents' GitHub token is stored
options.why: The broker gets its GitHub App key from Vault; the CI role is a different thing.

options.text: Because Vault cannot be changed once the pilot starts
options.why: Vault can change any time; the order is about what an agent branch could reach.

quiz.q: A ticket has the flag decide. What is it?

options.text: Optional work we do only if time allows
A choice with an owner, usually a meeting with no code
options.why: decide tickets end with a written decision that other tickets wait for.

options.text: A ticket that is blocked on another team
options.why: Blocking shows in deps and needs, not in the flag.

quiz.q: Renovate for dependencies (G5) starts in W5, before the agent runtime is ready. Why is that fine?

options.text: Because routines do not need walls
options.why: Routines need every wall Nova needs.

options.text: Because Renovate is a normal tool, not an agent; only the fixer routines that repair its PRs need the runtime
options.why: Work that runs no agent can start early. The fixers come later, on Nova's harness.

options.text: Because G5 has its own runtime separate from G3
options.why: Routines reuse Nova's harness, VMs and walls on purpose.

words.plain: One of the nine parts of the plan, G0 to G8, each a list of tickets.
The thirteen weeks of the quarter; W1 is 1 to 7 October 2026.
deps lists tickets in the same goal that go first; needs names what comes from other goals.
Flags: decide is a choice with an owner; stretch is done only if time allows.
A fixed set of past fcp tickets with hidden tests, used to score Nova.
The stages a routine climbs: shadow, then drafts to its owner, then normal.

tickets.why: The review rules are the first ticket of the quarter; every later wall enforces them.
The drills in W9 are the proof the runtime works before the pilot.
The pilot start shows how small and careful the first Nova tickets are.
The trust ladder is how a routine earns its way from shadow to normal.

remember: Walls first (G0), runtime second (G3), agents third (G4, G5); measurement, review, fast tests, skills and the brain feed the agents.
